JUDGMENT

The appellants have preferred this appeal under Sec.29 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, challenging the judgment passed by the learned MMTC-VI, Bengaluru, in Crl.Misc.No.2/2018 dated 12.01.2024.
2.

entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: The appellants are the respondents and respondents are the petitioners before the Trial Court.

For the purpose of convenience, the parties to this appeal are hereinafter referred to their rank in Crl.Misc.2/2018 before the Trial Court in this appeal since the respondents in the said petition have preferred this appeal.
The brief facts of the case is that, the petitioner No.1 is the mother of respondent No.1 and petitioner No.2.
Respondent No.2 is the daughter-in-law of petitioner No.1 and wife of respondent No.1.
It is stated that, the husband of petitioner No.1 died 26 years back.
During the year 2000, the respondent No.1 secured Government job on the basis of compassionate ground and he was residing with the petitioners till October 2017.
The petitioner No.1 has spent her entire life for respondent No.1 and petitioner No.2.
She even purchased car for respondent No.1 in the year 2014.
In the month of January 2017, the respondent No.1 mentally and physically tortured her by abusing her in filthy language and assaulted her and also threatened to take away her life.
Unable to tolerate the behaviour of the respondents, petitioners have filed complaint to the jurisdictional police several times, orally.
However, the police authorities have not taken any action against the respondents and they advised the petitioners to approach the Court.
In the month of November 2016, the marriage of respondent No.1 and 2 were solemnized and they were all residing in their house at Byatarayanapura, Sahakaranagar, Bengaluru.
Two months of their marriage, respondent No.2 started to harass petitioner No.1, assaulted her and even threatened to take away her life.

Thereafter, respondent No.2 left the matrimonial house and Crl.Apl.261/2024 went to her parents house stating that she will not reside in the said house unless petitioners are thrown out from their residence.

Respondent No.1 at the instigation of his wife has neglected the petitioners in all aspects has stopped maintaining the petitioners even though the petitioner No.2 is visually impaired and unmarried woman and petitioner No.1 is an aged lady, who is in need of medical treatment.

sentences.text: On 23.01.2017, respondent No.1 and 2 moved to a separate rented house at Amruthahalli and respondent No.1 has taken all the household things along with jewels of petitioner No.1, forcibly.
The respondent No.1 has completely deserted the petitioners and neglected them.
The petitioners are not in a position to get two meals a day.
The petitioner No.1 is suffering from age related ailments i.e., diabetes, B.P and she has undergone eye surgery.
Petitioner No.2 is visually impaired and she is depending on petitioner No.1 for her livelihood.
The petitioner No.1 is receiving pension of Rs.6,000/- p.m and she is in need of Rs.11,000/- p.m towards rent and basic necessities and medical expenses.
The respondent No.1 is working as a car driver at ADLR Office, K.G.Road, Bengaluru and he is getting salary of Rs.35,000/- p.m and he also owns agricultural lands.
Petitioner No.1 also Crl.Apl.261/2024 submits that, it is the moral and legal duty of respondent No.1 to maintain the petitioners.
Hence, the petitioner has filed the petition.

Upon receipt of the notice, the respondents appeared before the Trial Court and filed objections stating that, during his stay in Bengaluru, petitioners tortured him and petitioner No.1 was harassing respondent No.2 and humiliated her.

It is submitted that the respondent No.1 since 1983 to 1991 brought up by his maternal uncle by name Narayana Reddy, grandfather Sanjeeva Reddy and grandmother Lakshmamma at Maropalli Village, Pennagonda Taluk, Ananthpura District and thereafter lived with his uncle and only he started to reside with the petitioners from the date of death of his father i.e., 09-03-1993.
During the stay of respondent No.1 and 2 in the house of petitioners, petitioner No.1 tortured the respondents mentally and also inflicted cruelty against the respondents, using vulgar language which no ordinary mother and mother-in-law would use.
The petitioner No.1 was not allowing the respondent No.2 to enter the kitchen and she used to abuse her in filthy language.
Petitioner No.1 has not allowed respondent No.2 to purchase vegetables or any other daily needs and she used to scold respondent No.2 doubting her chastity and humiliated her.
On 17.10.2017, the petitioner No.1 picked up quarrel and went to the Police Station to lodge a complaint.
The SHO having Crl.Apl.261/2024 learnt about the facts advised the petitioner No.1 and asked respondent No.1 to set-up a separate house.

The respondent No.1 left with no option stayed in the house of the parents of respondent No.2 and on 22.10.2017 respondent No.1 visited the house of petitioner No.1 only to take back their belongings, however, he was not allowed to bring the gold ornaments of respondent No.2.
It is submitted that, the respondent No.2 went to her parent's house for delivery, however, it got aborted.
Since 14.05.2017 the respondent No.2 is not residing with the petitioners, so the question of picking up altercation on 17.10.2017 does not arise.

sentences.text: The petitioner No.1 is getting her husband's pension to the tune of Rs.13,000/- and 2nd petitioner is getting a pension of Rs.1,200/-.

Petitioner No.1 owns agricultural land to an extent of 2 acres 01 guntas in her name and 3 acres 3 guntas in the name of joint family and 34 guntas of wet land at Ittikadibbanahalli, Madhugiri Taluk, Tumkur District.
It is submitted that, the gross salary of respondent No.1 is around Rs.25,771/- and net salary is Rs.10,351/-.
The respondent No.2 is a house wife.

The respondent No.1 was forced to borrow a sum of Rs.1,00,000/- for interest at the rate of 2% p.m from Shivanna, towards advance to get rented house and he is paying an amount of Rs.5,500/- towards monthly rent and Rs.500/- towards water and electricity charges.

Earlier, when respondents and petitioners were living together the respondent No.1 had paid security deposit of Rs.60,000/- to the erstwhile landlord Seenappa and the said security deposit is received by petitioner No.1 while vacating the premises.

The respondent No.1 made an application in BSNL Central and State Government, IT/BT Employees (Working and Retired) HBCS Limited for allotment of site measuring 30 x 40 feet situated at Bettahalasur, Bengaluru, in the name of petitioner No.1 for a sale consideration of Rs.12,00,000/-.

The respondent No.1 has paid 3 installments i.e., sum of Rs.2,90,000/-,
Rs.2,85,000/- and Rs.2,85,000/- , totally amounting to Rs.8,60,000/- and the aforesaid site is intended to be given to petitioner No.2.
The respondent No.1 is paying Rs.1,300/- towards Life Insurance in the name of petitioner No.2 and the said insurance bond is in the custody of the petitioners.
Hence, prayed to dismiss the petition.

The Trial Court after full fledged trial, passed the order by allowing the petition in part and directed the respondent No.1 to pay an amount of Rs.5,000/- p.m each to the petitioners towards maintenance from the date of petition till their life time or till they get re-married whichever is earlier and respondent No.1 is also directed to pay an amount of Rs.5,000/- p.m to the petitioners towards rent Crl.Apl.261/2024 and to pay an amount of Rs.25,000/- to the petitioners towards medical expenses.
4. Being aggrieved by the said order the appellants/respondents have come up with this appeal on the following grounds :
1) The Trial Court failed to consider the fact that the respondents suppressed the fact that the first petitioner own lands at Ittikadibbanhalli, Madhugiri Taluk, to an extent of 5 acres, 37 guntas, apart from that she owned another land measuring 3 acres and she has sold the said land to Namadari Seeds Company since she had some financial difficulties.

2) The Trial Court has not appreciated the fact that respondent has paid sum of Rs.8,60,000/- installment amount towards allotment of site in the name of petitioner No.1.

Crl.Apl.261/2024 5) The Trial Court failed to consider the fact that the first petitioner had not paid amount of Rs.1,40,000/- to purchase a car as alleged, however, the said amount is paid by Sri.Balakrishna Naidu.

6) The respondent No.1 has produced the registered partition deed dated 10.12.2001 entered into between himself, the first petitioner and the second petitioner, who was a minor then, wherein, it has been specifically mentioned that from that day onwards the parties to the document shall not have any economical relationship except the blood relationship and the said documents has been marked in the evidence.
Hence, on these and amongst other grounds, the impugned judgment passed by the Trial Court below is liable to be set-aside in the interest of justice and equity.
5. This appeal was presented before the Honb'le Prl. City Civil & Sessions Judge, Bengaluru, it was registered as Criminal Appeal No.261/2024 and made over to this Court for disposal according to law.

Accordingly, prayed to vacate the interim order.
However, counsel for the respondents has not filed any objections.

7. Heard both the counsels and perused the materials placed before me.
8.

The points that arise for my consideration are as under:
1. Whether the appellant proves that impugned judgment dated 12.01.2024 is liable to be set-aside?
2. Whether the interference of this court is necessary in the impugned judgment of the trial court ?

sentences.text: 3 . What Order ?
POINT NO.1 :
The respondent has filed this appeal as against the order passed by the Trial Court in Crl.Misc.2/2018 dated 12.01.2024.

As per the memorandum of appeal, the petitioner No.1 and 2 are the mother and sister of respondent No.1 and he has filed the appeal by challenging order passed by the Trial Court directing him to pay Rs.5,000/- as maintenance to both the petitioners along with Rs.5,000/- p.m towards rent and Rs.25,000/- towards medical expenses.
11.
It is contended that, petitioner No.1 is receiving pension of her husband to the tune of around Rs.13,000/- p.m and petitioner No.2 is also getting Rs.1,300/- as she is blind.

It is also contended that the petitioner No.1 owns land in Madhugiri and partition is already affected between the petitioners and respondent No.1, wherein, it is stated that, there will be no economic relationship amongst them except their relationship by blood.
12.

Coming to the cross examination of PW.1, though it is contended that, she has purchased the second hand car for the use of respondent No.1, she clearly admitted that the said car is Crl.Apl.261/2024 registered in the name of Balakrishna Naidu, who is the friend of respondent No.1.
She has not produced any bank statement or any other documents to show that she has paid the amount to the purchase the car.
When the petitioner No.1 specifically contends that she purchased the car for respondent No.2, burden is upon her to prove the said fact.

Contrary to the said principle,
the Trial Court has observed that, it may be possible that the petitioner No.1 might have paid the amount since respondent No.1 is the Government employee and the Trial Court itself has opined that, the petitioner No.1 probably purchased the car and also opined that if at all said Balakrishna Naidu was examined, he would help his friend i.e., respondent No.1 deposing in his favour.

13. To prove that car was purchased by petitioner No.1, definitely duty is caste upon her to prove the same and Trial Court erred in presuming that he might have paid for it and the said Balakrishna Naidu would have deposed in favour of respondent No.1, which is bad in law.

Secondly, PW.1, clearly admitted that, as respondent No.2 left the matrimonial house on 14.05.2017, however, she filed complaint on 17.10.2017.
As such, it cannot be believed that respondent No.2 has picked up altercation with the petitioner on 17.10.2017 as stated in their petition.
The Trial Court has rightly Crl.Apl.261/2024 observed that respondent No.2 is not involved in the alleged incident which took place on 17.10.2017.

Though the said complaint filed by the petitioner No.1 was registered as N.C.R and as per the respondent No.1, on 22.10.2017 he shifted some household articles from the house of petitioner No.1 to his rented house.
Hence, it is clear that there was some dispute between petitioners and respondents on 17.10.2017 and hence, the respondent No.1 moved to rented house after the incident.

15. Though petitioner No.1 has stated that, the respondent No.1 took all the utensils without leaving any of them, as per the invoices produced by her at Ex.P.2, she has purchased a cooker, a fridge,
washing machine only in the year 2018.
If at all, the respondent has taken all the utensils on 22.10.2017, how the respondents survive without the utensils till 2018 remain unanswered.

16. Petitioners have also produced one of the invoice pertaining to the year 2014 and though it is stated by PW.1 that, the respondents have taken all her golden jewellery, it is not proved by her by producing relevant documents.

17. As per the documents available, it is apparent that everything was not good between the petitioners and the Crl.Apl.261/2024 respondents and it is also admitted that respondent No.2 has left their even month prior to the incident.

Though the petitioner O.1 has stated that she is received pension of Rs.6,000/- p.m and she will produced recent documents to that effect, she failed to produce recent statement with respect to the pension.
As per the respondents, petitioner No.1 is receiving pension of Rs.13,000/- p.m but she has not produced any documents.

18. Though both the parties to the suit have clearly admitted the partition deed i.e., Ex.R.1, wherein it is stated that the properties are divided amongst petitioners and respondent No.1 and from there will be no financial dependency amongst them.

19. One more point to be considered is that, as per Ex.R.3 i.e., case papers pertaining to C.C.No.24520/2017, wherein, the present petitioner No.1 is cited as CW.1 wherein, she gave statement on 12.06.2017 stating that she is running chit fund business with Chandrakala, who is the accused in that case, however, it cannot be relied upon and it is not a substantial piece of evidence.

20. Though the respondent No.1 has stated that he has paid installments of Rs.8,60,000/- with respect towards site intended to be purchased in the name of petitioner No.1 and premium amount Crl.Apl.261/2024 of Rs.1,300/- p.m in the name of petitioner No.2, these documents are not produced before the Court.

21. As per the petitioners they are in need of maintenance amount from day today affairs and also for medical expenses and she has also relied upon Ex.P.7 i.e., the rental agreement to show that the used to pay rent of Rs.7,300/-.

Though the petitioner No.1 has not produced the recent documents pertaining to her document, the Trial court has wrongly opined she is getting a meager amount of Manjunatha Reddy vs Subbamma on 4 October, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/94927289/
7 Rs.6,000/- and though she has 3 agricultural land, she is not able to derive income from the said land as she is old.

sentences.text: Petitioner No.1 ought to have produced the pension paper and when she owns land as per the partition deed, she would derive income in the aid land.
Hence, it is not necessary to cultivate the land by herself.
In the RTC produce by the respondents it is apparent that, the crops are mentioned in the said land.

22. Even the respondent has also produced the rental agreement at Ex.R.5 to show that he is residing in the premises on monthly rent of Rs.6,000/- as per his salary slip i.e., Ex.R.6 pertaining to the month of February 2018, his gross salary is Rs.25,771/- and net salary is Rs.10,951/-.
Though the Trial Court has stated the respondent No.1 has also produced the salary slip Crl.Apl.261/2024 pertaining to February 2022, it is not available and even it is not marked.

23. With respect to the salary of respondent No.1, the Trial Court has opined that his salary would have been increased by now, per contra Trial Court failed to take note that income of petitioner No.1 would have also increased by now.
24. The petitioners have also produced blind certificate and medical documents as per Ex.P.8 to P.13 pertaining to petitioner No.2 and petitioner No.1 to show that petitioner No.1 is diabetic.

25. By considering the circumstances and facts of the case in total, it is apparent that both petitioner No.1 and 2 have filed petition before the Trial Court seeking maintenance against respondent No.1 and as already discussed by me, no domestic violence is made out as alleged against respondent No.2 and even when it is admitted by both the parties to the petition as per the partition deed there will be no financial dependency amongst them, it is the moral duty of the son to lookafter his mother and sister, though the petitioners are getting pension.
26. On going through the entire petition, it is only stated that petitioner No.2 is blind and unmarried and it is also stated that, Crl.Apl.261/2024 respondent No.1 has neglected them.
No specific allegation are made against respondents to show that they have physically or mentally tortured petitioner No.2.
As per Ex.P.8 petitioner No.2 is blind but it is a fact that she is not blind because of the domestic violence as alleged in the petition.

It is the duty of petitioner No.1 to lookafter her daughter i.e., petitioner No.2 and moreover, as said by me earlier nowhere in the petition it is made out that the respondents made petitioner No.2 to physical abuse, mental abuse or economic abuse.
Even petitioner No.2 has failed to depose anything before the Court.

Though respondent No.1 is not legally required to lookafter petitioner No.2, as a brother, morally it is his duty to lookafter petitioner No.2 and it is relevant to say that, petitioner No.1 is also equally responsible to lookafter petitioner No.2.
27. Per contra, it is also necessary to consider the salary drawn by respondent No.1 and his duty to lookafter his wife and daughter as a duty bound husband.
28. To conclude, it is certain that being the son of petitioner No. and brother of petitioner No.2, it is the moral duty of respondent No.1 to lookafter both of them.

It is also his duty to maintain his wife and daughter and it is to be borne in mind that, he also residing in rented premises and he has local Manjunatha Reddy vs Subbamma on 4 October, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/94927289/
8 recovery.

Despite direction issued Crl.Apl.261/2024 by the Trial Court to produce pension papers,
petitioner No.1 failed to do so and even it is to be kept in mind that, the first wife of respondent No.1 has filed complaint U/Sec.498A of IPC alleging against the petitioner No.1 and the respondent No.1.

In this scenario, it is just to direct the respondent No.1 to pay maintenance amount of Rs.5,000/-
p.m to petitioner No.1, Rs.2,000/- p.m to petitioner No.2 along with Rs.4,000/- p.m towards rent.

Accordingly, I answer Point No.1 & 2 Partly in the Affirmative.
29.
Coming to the application dated 24.07.2024 filed by the petitioners, respondent No.1 to pay the maintenance as ordered by this Court from the date of petition, forthwith.
Hence, the application filed by the petitioners deserves to be allowed in part.
30. POINT NO.3 :

For the aforesaid reasons, I pass the following:
ORDER
The Criminal Appeal filed by the appellants under Sec.29 of Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, is hereby allowed in part.
